result.summary: Lecture 7 covers CPU scheduling. The scheduler picks which ready process runs next, and the dispatcher hands over the CPU through a context switch. Preemptive scheduling can take the CPU from a running process, while non-preemptive scheduling lets it run until it blocks or finishes. First-Come First-Served is simple but suffers the convoy effect. Shortest Job First gives the minimum average waiting time but needs burst prediction and can starve long processes. Round Robin gives each process a fixed time quantum; a very large quantum behaves like FCFS and a very small one is dominated by context-switch overhead. Priority scheduling can cause starvation, which aging solves by gradually raising the priority of waiting processes. Key metrics are turnaround time (completion minus arrival), waiting time (turnaround minus burst) and response time (first run minus arrival).

Scheduling that runs the process with the smallest next CPU burst; it minimises average waiting time but can starve long processes.
Scheduling in which each process gets a fixed time quantum and then goes to the back of the ready queue.
The fixed amount of CPU time a process gets in Round Robin before it is preempted.
Gradually increasing the priority of waiting processes to prevent starvation.

questions.question: What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is very large or very small?

questions.question: How does aging solve starvation in priority scheduling?
questions.answer: It gradually increases the priority of waiting processes.

questions.answer: Turnaround time is 10 and waiting time is 4.

result.summary: Lecture 2 introduces algorithm analysis and Big-O notation. Time complexity describes how running time grows with input size n, not the exact number of seconds. Big-O gives an upper bound: f(n) = O(g(n)) if constants c and n0 exist such that f(n) <= c*g(n) for all n >= n0. Common growth classes, in increasing order, are O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2) and O(2^n). Constants and lower-order terms are dropped, so 3n^2 + 5n + 7 is O(n^2). Binary search is O(log n) and linear search is O(n). Merge sort is O(n log n) in the worst case, and insertion sort is O(n^2) in the worst case but O(n) on sorted input. Big-Omega gives a lower bound, Big-Theta gives a tight bound, and space complexity measures extra memory as a function of n.

result.summary: Lecture 11 covers database normalization, the process of organizing tables to reduce redundancy and avoid update, insertion and deletion anomalies. A functional dependency X -> Y means each value of X determines exactly one value of Y. The normal forms build on each other: 1NF requires atomic values and no repeating groups; 2NF requires 1NF plus no partial dependency on part of a composite key; 3NF requires 2NF plus no transitive dependency between non-key attributes; and BCNF requires that the left side of every functional dependency be a superkey. A transitive dependency is resolved by splitting the table, as in Student and Department. Denormalization deliberately reintroduces redundancy to speed up reads, at the cost of more complex updates.

The table is in 2NF and no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute.
A stricter form in which, for every functional dependency X -> Y, X is a superkey.
A case where a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, which 3NF removes.
A set of attributes that uniquely identifies each row in a table.

result.summary: Lecture 14 covers TCP connection management. TCP is a connection-oriented, reliable, byte-stream protocol that provides ordered delivery and retransmits lost segments. A connection opens with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and closes with a four-way teardown using FIN and ACK in each direction. Sequence numbers label bytes so the receiver can reorder data and detect loss, and ACKs confirm what was received. Flow control uses the receiver's advertised window (rwnd) to avoid overwhelming its buffer. Congestion control protects the network: slow start grows the congestion window (cwnd) roughly exponentially until the slow-start threshold (ssthresh), then congestion avoidance grows it by about one segment per round trip. On a timeout, TCP halves cwnd into ssthresh and restarts slow start. UDP, by contrast, is connectionless and offers no delivery guarantee.

A message telling the sender what data the receiver has received.
Limiting the sender's rate so it does not overwhelm the receiver's buffer, using the advertised window (rwnd).
The sender-side limit on how much unacknowledged data may be in flight, used for congestion control.
A congestion control phase in which cwnd starts small and roughly doubles every round trip until it reaches ssthresh.
The cwnd value at which slow start ends and congestion avoidance begins.
A phase in which cwnd increases by about one segment per round trip.
Closing a TCP connection by exchanging FIN and ACK segments in each direction.
A connectionless transport protocol that gives no delivery guarantee.

questions.answer: SYN from the client, SYN-ACK from the server, and ACK from the client.

questions.question: What is the difference between flow control and congestion control in TCP?
questions.answer: Flow control protects the receiver's buffer and uses the advertised window (rwnd). Congestion control protects the network and uses the congestion window (cwnd).

questions.question: How does TCP grow cwnd during slow start and during congestion avoidance?
questions.answer: During slow start cwnd roughly doubles every round trip until it reaches ssthresh. During congestion avoidance it increases by about one segment per round trip.

questions.question: What does TCP do to ssthresh and cwnd when a timeout indicates packet loss?
questions.answer: It sets ssthresh to half of cwnd and restarts slow start.

questions.question: How is a TCP connection closed?
questions.answer: With a four-way teardown: FIN and ACK segments are exchanged in each direction.

questions.question: How does UDP differ from TCP in terms of delivery?
questions.answer: UDP is connectionless and gives no delivery guarantee, whereas TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery.

result.summary: Lecture 5 covers gradient descent, an optimization method that minimises a loss function L(w) by repeatedly moving the parameters w opposite to the gradient. The update rule is w_new = w_old - alpha * dL/dw, where alpha is the learning rate. A learning rate that is too small makes convergence slow, and one that is too large can overshoot and diverge. Batch gradient descent uses the whole training set per step and is stable but slow on large data. Stochastic gradient descent uses one example per update, which is fast and noisy, and the noise can help escape shallow local minima. Mini-batch gradient descent uses a small batch, such as 32 or 64 examples, and is the usual practice. For convex losses such as mean squared error in linear regression, gradient descent with a suitable learning rate reaches the global minimum. Feature scaling such as standardisation speeds convergence, and an epoch is one full pass through the training data.

result.summary: Lecture 3 introduces the basics of prompting. The output quality of a language model depends strongly on how the prompt is written. Zero-shot prompting gives an instruction with no examples, while few-shot prompting includes input-output examples so the model can imitate the pattern and format. A good prompt states the role, task, context, constraints and required output format. Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason step by step, which often helps arithmetic and logic. Hallucination is fluent but unsupported or false output, and grounding the model in provided documents and asking it to quote sources reduces it. Temperature controls randomness: low temperature is more deterministic and high temperature is more varied. Prompt injection occurs when untrusted input tries to override the developer's instructions. Prompts should be tested on a fixed test set and versioned like code.

questions.question: What is the difference between a logical address and a physical address, and which hardware performs the translation?
questions.answer: A logical (virtual) address is generated by the program. The MMU translates it into a physical address in main memory.

questions.question: When is execution-time address binding needed?
questions.answer: It is needed when a process can be moved in memory while it runs.

questions.question: How do base and limit registers provide protection?
questions.answer: Every address generated by a process is checked against the base and limit registers. An illegal access causes a trap to the operating system.

questions.question: What is the difference between first-fit, best-fit and worst-fit?
questions.answer: First-fit allocates the first hole that is large enough, best-fit the smallest hole that is large enough, and worst-fit the largest hole. First-fit and best-fit are usually better than worst-fit in speed and storage use.

questions.question: What is the difference between external and internal fragmentation?
questions.answer: External fragmentation means enough total free memory exists but is split into holes that are too small. Internal fragmentation means allocated memory is larger than requested, so the unused space inside the block is wasted.

questions.question: Why does paging avoid external fragmentation, and where can it still occur?
questions.answer: Paging uses fixed-size frames, so there is no external fragmentation. Internal fragmentation can still occur in the last page of a process.

questions.question: On average, how much memory is wasted per process due to internal fragmentation in paging, and how does page size affect this?
questions.answer: About half a page per process. A smaller page size wastes less but makes the page table larger.

questions.question: Why does paging slow down memory access without a TLB?
questions.answer: The page table is kept in main memory, so each memory reference needs two accesses: one for the page table and one for the data.

questions.question: What happens on a TLB hit and on a TLB miss?
questions.answer: On a hit, the frame number is available immediately. On a miss, the page table in memory is consulted and the entry is loaded into the TLB.

questions.question: Calculate the effective access time with a TLB lookup of 10 ns, a memory access of 100 ns and a hit ratio of 80 percent.
What happens to effective access time as the hit ratio increases?
questions.answer: It moves closer to the cost of a single memory access.

questions.question: Why is a multi-level page table useful for a 32-bit address space?
questions.answer: A 32-bit address space with small pages needs a very large page table. A multi-level page table pages the table itself, so only the parts in use must be kept in memory.

questions.question: What is a logical address in segmentation, and what does a segment table store?
questions.answer: A logical address is a segment number and an offset. The segment table stores the base and limit of each segment.

questions.question: What causes a segmentation fault?
questions.answer: An offset beyond the segment limit causes a trap, commonly seen as a segmentation fault.

questions.question: Why does virtual memory work?
questions.answer: Because of locality of reference: programs tend to use a small set of pages at a time, so only part of a process needs to be in memory.

questions.question: What steps does the OS take on a page fault?
questions.answer: It finds a free frame, reads the page from disk into the frame, updates the page table, and restarts the instruction. If there is no free frame, a page replacement algorithm chooses a victim page.

questions.question: Why does the page fault rate strongly affect performance?
questions.answer: A disk read is far slower than a memory access.

questions.question: What is Belady's anomaly and which algorithm can exhibit it?
questions.answer: It is the situation where giving a process more frames increases the number of page faults. FIFO can exhibit it. For the reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, FIFO causes 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 faults with 4 frames.

questions.question: Why is the optimal page replacement algorithm not implemented in practice?
questions.answer: It needs knowledge of future references, so it cannot be implemented. It is used as a benchmark.

questions.question: How does LRU approximate the optimal algorithm, and what hardware support does it need?
questions.answer: LRU replaces the page not used for the longest time, looking at the past instead of the future. It needs a hardware counter or a stack of page numbers.

questions.question: What is thrashing and why can it get worse?
questions.answer: Thrashing happens when a process does not have enough frames for its active pages, so it spends more time paging than executing. CPU utilisation falls, and a scheduler may admit more processes, which makes the problem worse.

questions.question: How does the working-set model decide how many frames a process needs?
questions.answer: It uses the pages referenced in the most recent window of references.

questions.question: How can thrashing be limited?
questions.answer: By reducing the degree of multiprogramming or by suspending some processes.

It starts with splitting data into training, validation and test sets, and warns about test-set reuse and data leakage. It then covers overfitting, underfitting and the bias-variance trade-off, with regularization and early stopping as remedies. K-fold cross-validation gives a more stable estimate. For classifiers, the lecture introduces the confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall and F1, and explains why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data. It then covers thresholds, the ROC curve and AUC, and regression metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE and R squared). It closes with a practical checklist.

questions.question: What are the purposes of the training, validation and test sets?
questions.answer: The training set fits model parameters, the validation set chooses hyperparameters and compares models, and the test set is used once at the end to estimate performance on new data.

questions.question: Why does repeatedly using the test set to tune a model make its score optimistic?
questions.answer: The test data has indirectly influenced the model, so the score no longer reflects new data.

questions.question: What is data leakage and what effect does it have?
questions.answer: Data leakage is when information from outside the training data, such as the test set or the future, is used to build the model. It produces unrealistically good results that disappear in real use.

questions.question: How do underfitting and overfitting differ in their errors?
questions.answer: Underfitting has high error on both training and test data. Overfitting has very low training error but much higher error on new data.

questions.question: What does the bias-variance trade-off say about making a model more complex?
questions.answer: Making a model more complex usually lowers bias and raises variance. High bias leads to underfitting and high variance leads to overfitting.

questions.question: How do L1 and L2 regularization differ?
questions.answer: L2 penalises the sum of squared weights. L1 penalises the sum of absolute weights and can drive some weights to exactly zero.

questions.question: What is early stopping?
questions.answer: Halting training when the validation error stops improving.

questions.question: How does k-fold cross-validation work?
questions.answer: The data is divided into k equal folds. The model is trained k times, each time holding out one fold for validation and training on the other k minus 1 folds. The k scores are averaged.

questions.question: What are the advantages and the cost of cross-validation?
questions.answer: It gives a more stable estimate than a single split and is useful when data is limited, but it costs k times more training.

questions.question: What are the four outcomes in a binary confusion matrix?
questions.answer: True positive (positive predicted positive), false positive (negative predicted positive), false negative (positive predicted negative) and true negative (negative predicted negative).

questions.question: What is the formula for precision and what does it answer?
questions.answer: Precision is TP divided by (TP + FP). It answers: of the examples predicted positive, how many really are positive?

questions.question: What is the formula for recall and what does it answer?
questions.answer: Recall is TP divided by (TP + FN). It answers: of the really positive examples, how many did the model find?

questions.question: How is F1 score calculated and when is it high?
questions.answer: F1 is 2 x precision x recall divided by (precision + recall), the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is high only when both precision and recall are high.

questions.question: Why is accuracy misleading when 99 percent of examples are negative?
questions.answer: A model that always predicts negative gets 99 percent accuracy but finds no positive cases.

questions.question: Which metric should be emphasised in disease screening, and which in spam filtering?
questions.answer: Recall in disease screening, where a false negative is usually worse. Precision in spam filtering, where a false positive may be worse.

questions.question: What happens to precision and recall when the classification threshold is raised?
questions.answer: Precision usually increases and recall usually decreases.

questions.question: What is the false positive rate?
questions.answer: FP divided by (FP + TN).

questions.question: What does the ROC curve plot and what does AUC summarise?
questions.answer: The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate for every threshold. AUC summarises performance across thresholds.

questions.question: What do AUC values of 0.5 and 1.0 mean?
questions.answer: 0.5 corresponds to random guessing and 1.0 to a perfect ranking.

questions.question: How do MSE and RMSE differ from MAE in sensitivity to errors?
questions.answer: Squaring makes MSE and RMSE more sensitive to large errors than MAE. RMSE is the square root of MSE and is in the same units as the target.

questions.question: What does R squared measure?
questions.answer: The proportion of the variance in the target that the model explains. A value of 0 means the model does no better than predicting the mean.

questions.question: What should be done before preprocessing to avoid leakage?
questions.answer: Split the data before any preprocessing that learns from it.

questions.question: What is the difference between functional and non-functional requirements?
questions.answer: Functional requirements say what the system must do. Non-functional requirements say how well it must do it.

questions.question: Why is maintenance an important phase in the SDLC?
questions.answer: Maintenance often costs more than the first development.

questions.question: What is the main weakness of the waterfall model?
questions.answer: Feedback comes late and changing requirements is expensive.

questions.question: When does the waterfall model suit a project?
questions.answer: It suits projects with stable, well-understood requirements.

questions.question: How does Agile differ from waterfall in how it delivers software?
questions.answer: Agile is iterative and incremental, delivering working software in short cycles with customer feedback after every iteration, and it adjusts plans as requirements change.

questions.question: What are the four values of the Agile Manifesto?
questions.answer: Individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, and responding to change.

questions.question: What are the responsibilities of the Product Owner and the Scrum Master?
questions.answer: The Product Owner owns the product backlog and decides priorities. The Scrum Master helps the team follow Scrum and removes obstacles.

questions.question: What is the difference between the product backlog and the sprint backlog?
questions.answer: The product backlog is an ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product. The sprint backlog holds the items chosen for the current sprint plus the plan to deliver them.

questions.question: What is an increment in Scrum?
questions.answer: The usable, potentially releasable result of a sprint.

questions.question: What happens in a sprint review and a sprint retrospective?
questions.answer: In the sprint review the team shows the increment to stakeholders. In the retrospective the team reflects on how to improve its process.

questions.question: How long is a daily scrum and what is its purpose?
questions.answer: It is a 15-minute meeting to synchronise the work.

questions.question: What is the difference between unit testing and integration testing?
questions.answer: Unit testing tests a single function or class in isolation, while integration testing tests that components work together.

questions.question: What does system testing check, and who performs acceptance testing?
questions.answer: System testing checks the complete system against the requirements. Acceptance testing is performed by the customer, who checks that the system meets their needs.

questions.question: What is the difference between black-box and white-box testing?
questions.answer: Black-box testing tests behaviour from inputs and outputs without looking at the code. White-box testing designs tests from the internal structure of the code, for example to cover every branch.

questions.question: What is regression testing?
questions.answer: Re-running earlier tests after a change to make sure nothing that worked has broken.

questions.question: What is the difference between a branch and a merge in version control?
questions.answer: A branch is a separate line of development. A merge combines branches.

questions.question: What is a code review and why is it useful?
questions.answer: Another developer inspects changes before they are merged. It finds defects early and shares knowledge.

questions.question: What does continuous integration involve?
questions.answer: Developers merge small changes often, and each merge triggers an automated build and test run.

questions.question: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
questions.answer: In continuous delivery every passing change is kept in a releasable state. In continuous deployment every passing change is released to users automatically.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of continuous integration?
questions.answer: Problems are found within minutes of being introduced.

questions.question: What is technical debt and how is it reduced?
questions.answer: Technical debt is shortcuts in design or code that make later changes harder, and it accumulates interest as the code grows. It is reduced by refactoring, tests and code review.
